messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Walter, a 77-year-old North American man, came to treatment after months of trying to carry on as if nothing had changed since the assault that disrupted his sense of safety and competence. He had been married for many years and was still working as a delivery driver, a job that kept him on the road, moving from one stop to the next and giving him a routine he could organize himself around. The attack happened in the context of that ordinary workday. While making a delivery, he was confronted and assaulted in a way that left him frightened and shaken, and what stayed with him most was not only the violence itself but the abrupt realization that the situation had turned dangerous before he could sort out what to do. In the months after, Walter found himself replaying the event in a way that made him feel as though he were back in it, but he fought hard to keep those moments from coming into view. He would say to himself that he had to push it away, because if he let his mind go there he would not be able to handle it. When the memory threatened to surface, he would cut it off quickly, redirecting his attention to whatever task was in front of him.

That determination to stay occupied became one of his main strategies. Walter began working even harder at keeping busy, filling his days with errands, chores, and anything that would prevent stillness. At home he would keep moving from one task to another, not because he wanted to be productive alone, but because quiet moments made him feel exposed to what he was trying not to think about. He noticed that if he sat too long, his mind would drift toward the assault, and he became wary of any pause that might leave him alone with it. He also found himself eating far more than usual, often grazing through the evening in a way that gave him a brief sense of relief. He described overeating as something he did to manage the distress that built up in him, especially after a day in which he had spent so much effort keeping the event out of mind.

The assault altered the way Walter understood himself and the world. He spoke with a troubling lack of confidence about his own judgment, saying that he could no longer trust himself to do the right thing if something unexpected happened again. He had once seen himself as capable and steady on the job, able to make quick decisions and look after himself, but now he questioned whether he would respond correctly if he were put in danger. That doubt was tied to a larger feeling that the rules he had relied on were gone. He said that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed, and he meant it in a literal, everyday sense: the assumption that most people and most places were manageable no longer seemed reliable to him. A routine delivery route, a doorstep, a stranger’s tone of voice, or a sudden shift in a situation could all feel loaded now because he no longer trusted the basic order of things.

At work, Walter’s need to stay busy made it easier to keep going from stop to stop, but the job also kept placing him in situations that reminded him how vulnerable he had felt during the assault. He continued to deliver goods, but he was more guarded at each address and more likely to hurry through interactions so he could get back to the safety of his truck. He did not speak about the event to coworkers and did not want to burden his wife with too much of it, preferring to keep the subject out of conversation altogether. Over time, this left him feeling more alone with it. The efforts to suppress thoughts, fill time, and eat to settle himself had become part of his daily life, and despite all of it the distress remained close beneath the surface. By the time he finally sought help, Walter was not asking for his past to be erased; he was asking because he was weary of living as though one violent encounter had overturned everything he thought he knew. What frightened him most was the possibility that he would never regain confidence in his own judgment, and what he hoped for was some way to think about the assault without feeling that it would overwhelm him.
